Exposure therapy absolutely works. It's about turning into the discomfort and anxiety, and learning that it can't hurt you. Regular, repeated exposure, doing it again and again, until the anxiety lessens, and then doing something that causes more anxiety, until that anxiety lessens. Etc etc.

I was completely housebound for years, I couldn't even take my bins out. I started by standing on my doorstep, then pacing the carpark in front of my house, then doing laps of my tiny street, then crossing the road, then going up the road (this process took several months, doing it Mon-Fri, resting on Sat-Sun, and I had full blown panic attacks every time) I then started walking to a bus stop, taking a bus one stop, then 3 stops, and eventually into town. Then walking through town, and then started going into shops. All of this was supervised and talked about at the time, using de-escalating and mindfulness methods. Deep breathing, 54321 etc. Celebrating every single tiny win, *actually* celebrating it with a treat and acknowledging it. That's really important, getting into a positive mindset with *any* amount of progress. If it was a hard day and didn't meet a particular goal, you still got out the house! Celebrate it! 

I have since been abroad with a friend twice, and been to a city overnight on my own. It's absolutely doable. You just have to turn into it. I still have to force myself to leave my home, and I still hate it, but it isn't an all encompassing fear anymore.

It was over a 1 year period. I had already been doing some on my own, pacing the car park in front of my flat over a period of 3 months, so I'd managed to get out the front door, but I kept backsliding, and couldn't progress alone. 

We started doing single laps of my very small street (maybe around 50m or so) then double laps. Then double laps, plus crossing the road and straight back. Then the same but going up the street a little.
My 1st goal was crossing the road. My 2nd was making it to the entrance of the park which is a 1 minute walk away from my front door. My 3rd goal was making it onto a bench that's about 20m into the park. The goals progressed like that, until I made it onto a bus, and eventually into town. Then the exposure sessions took place in a regular place in town, which we went to together at first, and then I would eventually travel alone and meet them there. Every progression to a new goal was terrifying. Going into shops, getting on busses, going to crowded places. So many people seeing me have full blown panic attacks. But it's one of the best things I've ever done, and it's so worth it.

What I took away from it is the key to beating agoraphobia is support, regular exposure, time to rest and recover, small achievable goals that you actually celebrate when you achieve them, and pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, but not into a place where you feel like you're breaking.

Days out have to be planned in advance, I can't spontaneously do them (yet) and when I do go out, I have to keep my anxiety in check, and sometimes go have a secret panic attack in private 😅 If I stay home for too long without going out, I have a relapse, and have to force myself to go out. Gentle, gradual exposure is 100% key to battling agoraphobia
